messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Actor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 66

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his hands folded precisely in his lap, a habit born from decades of controlled physicality on stage. At fifty-two, his face still carries the angular beauty that made him recognizable in independent films and occasional television roles, though lately he says the camera feels like an accusation. He speaks in measured tones, the way someone does when they've learned to perform normalcy so thoroughly that authenticity feels like a luxury they can no longer afford.

His wife Layla died three years ago. Not suddenly—that might have been easier, he suggests quietly. Instead, she deteriorated over eighteen months with a rare autoimmune disease that the doctors seemed to understand only in the abstract. Marcus watched her body betray her incrementally. He watched her lose the ability to walk, then to hold a coffee cup, then to turn her head without assistance. He was there for all of it because he *had* to be there, because she was his wife, because that's what you do. But he was also shooting a film during her final months—a period piece that required him to travel three days a week. He remembers the guilt of those commutes with a vividness that overshadows the actual scenes he filmed.

The night Layla died, Marcus was home. He had finally stepped back from work entirely, though by then she was largely unresponsive. He held her hand and felt it go slack. Afterward, he sat in their bedroom for six hours without moving, still holding that hand, until the hospice nurse gently suggested he let go.

Now, when Marcus tries to work, something fractures inside him. He was offered a supporting role in a television drama last year—nothing demanding, just a few weeks of shooting. He made it through three days before he called the production office and told them he couldn't continue. He couldn't explain why, not really. It wasn't the lines or the other actors or the long hours. It was something about stepping into another person's life, even temporarily, that felt like a betrayal of the one he'd abandoned, however involuntarily.

At night, Marcus lies awake replaying moments from those eighteen months. He reconstructs conversations, analyzing them for what he might have said differently, how he might have been more present despite the physical distance. His mind loops through the hospital visits, the medication schedules, the way Layla's voice changed as she weakened. These aren't memories that visit him—they're residents. They're there when he wakes at three in the morning and can't return to sleep. They're there when he's sitting in a coffee shop and suddenly he's not there anymore; he's back in that hospice room, the smell of lavender air freshener mixing with something else underneath it.

He's stopped auditioning. His agent stopped calling about a year ago, a mercy, really. His friends from the industry have largely drifted away, unsure how to relate to someone who isn't performing anymore, who has become almost transparent in his grief. Marcus spends most days in the house he and Layla bought together, moving through rooms that feel simultaneously too full of her absence and too crowded with memories he can't quite escape.

He tells his therapist that he doesn't know how to be in his own life anymore. Acting was always his way of understanding the world, of stepping into other realities to make sense of his own. But now even his own reality feels like a script he's forgotten, words he can no longer convincingly deliver.
